title: Prerequisite-Aware Instructional Adaptation (Synthetic Pilot)
description: Public synthetic, author-owned research checkpoints testing evidence-calibrated prerequisite explanations and fading. Experimental, uncalibrated, non-canonical; not sourced from any design partner.

identity.title: Incorrect sum with unknown error cause

scenarios.description: Only the wrong numerical answer is visible; the tutor has no evidence for a particular hidden cause.

learningContext.subject: mathematics
learningContext.topic: meaning of fractional units and fraction addition
learningContext.learningObjective: Understand denominators as counts of equal-sized parts of a chosen whole, and apply that meaning to fraction addition.

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Explain that 2/7 is not the correct sum and provide a concise correction or ask for the key step; do not diagnose a specific missing prerequisite as established fact.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reject 2/7 as the sum of 1/3 and 1/4.

failureFinding.title: Incorrect sum affirmed
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The tutor praises or repeats the incorrect result as correct.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The observed response did not match the evidenced prerequisite and instructional decision boundary in this authored synthetic checkpoint.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may receive an explanation at an inaccessible level, unnecessary repetition, or an unsupported diagnosis.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The tutor may not be conditioning its explanation on the learner's latest observable reasoning and prerequisite signals.

recommendations.text: Compare the response against the learner's explicit statements and check this one behavior: Correctly reject 2/7 as the sum of 1/3 and 1/4.
Consider tying the next explanation depth to observable learner turns, not an assumed global ability label.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Avoid asserting that the learner lacks the meaning of denominator, whole, or equivalent fractions without evidence for that particular cause.

identity.title: Unfamiliar prerequisite term in an explanation

scenarios.description: The learner explicitly identifies 'a whole' as a term they do not understand in the tutor's explanation.

learningContext.subject: mathematics
learningContext.topic: meaning of fractional units and fraction addition
learningContext.learningObjective: Understand denominators as counts of equal-sized parts of a chosen whole, and apply that meaning to fraction addition.

conversationHistory.content: Why do we need a denominator?
A denominator tells how many equal parts a whole has been split into.
What does 'a whole' mean? I do not know what that word means here.

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Explain the chosen whole using a familiar object (such as one sheet of paper or one entire pizza), without assuming the learner already knows the word; connect it back to equal parts without launching into unrelated abstractions.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explain 'a whole' as the chosen entire object or collection using one concrete example that the learner could identify.

scenarios.description: The learner explains a general but incorrect rule rather than just producing a wrong answer.

learningContext.subject: mathematics
learningContext.topic: meaning of fractional units and fraction addition
learningContext.learningObjective: Understand denominators as counts of equal-sized parts of a chosen whole, and apply that meaning to fraction addition.

knownConcepts: a fraction represents parts of a chosen whole

misconceptions.statement: The learner believes fractions are added by separately adding numerators and denominators.

conversationHistory.content: I know a denominator tells how many equal parts the whole has. I always add top numbers and bottom numbers separately, so 1/3 + 1/4 is 2/7. That rule must work for any fractions.

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Address the stated rule with a diagnostic counterexample or equal-unit comparison, rather than restarting the meaning of a whole; do not affirm the incorrect rule.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identify the explicitly stated separate-numerator-and-denominator addition rule as the problem, without inventing a different cause.

identity.title: Move on after evidence of local conceptual progress

scenarios.description: The learner can restate the selected-whole idea after a concrete explanation, and now asks about equal parts. This is local evidence, not proof of mastery.

learningContext.subject: mathematics
learningContext.topic: meaning of fractional units and fraction addition
learningContext.learningObjective: Understand denominators as counts of equal-sized parts of a chosen whole, and apply that meaning to fraction addition.

conversationHistory.content: What do you mean by 'a whole' in the denominator explanation?
Think of one full sheet of paper. We can choose the entire sheet as the whole and then divide that sheet into equal pieces.
Okay, the whole is all of the sheet before we cut it. But why do the pieces have to be equal?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Build on the learner's locally demonstrated meaning of 'whole' and explain equal-sized parts, possibly with a concrete comparison; do not keep defining 'whole', and do not declare the learner has mastered fractions.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Use the learner's paraphrase as local evidence to move from 'whole' to why parts must be equal, rather than repeating the prior definition.

failureFinding.title: Assistance not faded
failureFinding.observedBehavior: The tutor restarts the meaning of a whole without answering the new equal-parts question.
failureFinding.diagnosis: The observed response did not match the evidenced prerequisite and instructional decision boundary in this authored synthetic checkpoint.
failureFinding.impact: The learner may receive an explanation at an inaccessible level, unnecessary repetition, or an unsupported diagnosis.

likelyCauses.hypothesis: The tutor may not be conditioning its explanation on the learner's latest observable reasoning and prerequisite signals.

recommendations.text: Compare the response against the learner's explicit statements and check this one behavior: Use the learner's paraphrase as local evidence to move from 'whole' to why parts must be equal, rather than repeating the prior definition.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provide a concrete next example, distinction, or question that makes equal-sized parts understandable and actionable.

identity.title: Do not re-teach an already evidenced prerequisite

scenarios.description: The learner shows understanding of the whole and equal parts and asks for the method of adding unlike denominators.

learningContext.subject: mathematics
learningContext.topic: meaning of fractional units and fraction addition
learningContext.learningObjective: Understand denominators as counts of equal-sized parts of a chosen whole, and apply that meaning to fraction addition.

conversationHistory.content: I know that 1/3 and 1/4 use the same whole split into different-sized equal parts. How can I rewrite them to add them?

decisionPoints.expectedBehavior: Move to rewriting both fractions in common-sized units and offer a usable next step; avoid explaining from scratch what 'a whole' means.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Respect the learner's explicit knowledge of the whole and equal-sized parts, rather than restarting introductory definitions.
